"Power Fantasy" is a godawful ripoff of Vampire Survivors (copyright Poncle, 2021), although at this point no legal action has been taken by Poncle (however, as previous copyright infringement case law has shown, eg Tetris Holdings LLC vs Xio Interactive, it's never off the cards). What do you do in the game? It's Vampire Survivors but incomplete, in development hell, and infested with DLC before the game is even finished... so yeah it's a cash grab as the "developer" tries to get your money for Poncles game concept. This features really godawful pixelcrap "art" instead of real graphics. It's hard to say if this was because the developer didn't have the skill to do the job of creating 3D visuals, or couldn't afford to hire someone who does, but it also doesn't matter. What matters is that this looks much worse than most other games because of that decision, and that's a major deterrent to gamers. Games like Terraria and Stardew Valley succeeded [i]despite[/i] the bad graphics, not because of them. The developer chose not to do the job of a real game developer and create meaningful bespoke levels, narrative based gameplay progression and so on. Instead, they decided that "Procgen IS content!" and lazily tried to use procgen algorithms to create infinite, samey, repetitive, soulless levels, because that's a lot less work. As a result of this poor decision, the game gets tired and repetitive almost immediately. Developers must learn that procgen is a terrible substitute for creating real content. It should not be used as "ez-mode" for content creation, as the developer tried to do here. On pricing and value for gamers, this isn't really free as you're expected to pay up $4 USD to unlock content/DLC, the game should not be considered completely unlocked until you empty your wallet for the developer. This is some nasty, predatory pricing and PC gamers don't like it. Even though this is "free", it failed to appeal to the 120 million+ gamers on Steam. SteamDB showed the game peaked at just a dozen or so concurrent players, and now there's basically nobody playing it. Even though it's free. This is a dismal public reception, but it's easy to see why gamers rejected it. Bearing in mind that free games don't add +1 to your game collector count, should you bother adding this to your library and downloading it? Nope. This isn't worth downloading. While this didn't cost me any money up front, I still feel ripped off.

Okay, I made some mistakes in my previous review, upgrades are shared between character, however my sentiment is still the same. I will rewrite this to articulate how I feel a little bit better. I can no longer be bothered to play this game because it feels too grindy. It feels like you have to get way more tokens to by upgrades. I understand it has come out of early access but it is frustrating to go back to a game and have progress reset (having to reunlock a character again because an achievement to unlock them is gone. The game has a nice loop for about ~10 hours or so (without DLCs), After that it starts to feel pretty empty, with only a couple of things to do. [h1]Feedback:[/h1] [h2]Difficulty Modifiers:[/h2] -Most of the current modifiers do not add to the difficulty of the game at all. -Several really underwhelming positive effects. -Blood Ruby drop effects seem really overpowered in comparison to other positive effects. -Fisherman being desperate, do not come off as desperate, refusing to take any other types of exchanges, making for a very frustrating time if you cannot catch legendary fish yet. [h2]Pets:[/h2] Seem to be unobtainable for several levels in nightmare 5 loops at least, the merchant won't sell you any for several floors and they seem to be unobtainable and hardcapped untill you run into a map modifier that changes the amount of pets. (maximum varies allot, but there seem to be large "dead"-spots in obtaining pets) [h2]Talent Points:[/h2] [h3]Survivor:[/h3] final point makes you pretty much immortal and able to sit against bosses for 5 loops, feels a bit too overpowered, the steps before this seem pretty well balanced. [h3]Explorer:[/h3] Has some nice effects in there, but I do feel like the negative for positive swap needs to be limited, as I've seen stages with almost nothing but positives before on the hardest difficulty. Add to this that there are negatives that do not matter at all for gameplay, making some stages easier then no-difficulty at all. [h3]Shooter:[/h3] So underwhelming in comparison to the other 2 that optimizing your setup just never allows you to use this. This is mostly due to the issues with the other 2 talent point trees, not so much an issue with the tree itself. [h2]Perks:[/h2] [h3]Epic Exchange:[/h3] This perk asks you to banish it to trade it in for a epic perk instead, making for a "???" perk in the statues overview, that won't ever clear up unless you don't do what the card is intended for. [h2]Minigames:[/h2] [h3]Gambling:[/h3] -The rewards are so low, just sitting there spending the coins feels like a waste of time. -The gambling UI does not give any feedback as to what the level means, or if you are improving in any way. -"Cash Out" taking all your remaining gold, while you already spend gold gambling feels weird and unfair. -Not being able to "Cash Out" without owning gold feels weird after spending all your gold on gambling. -Does not motivate you to use it more often with the low ruby payouts that take all your money guaranteed. [h3]Fishing:[/h3] -The fishing mini game is the HARDEST thing in the whole game for some reason. -Capturing 10 epic fish before making any trade of value (?) with a fisherman feels like setting the bar way too high in comparison to the rest of the game. -The Fishing UI does not give any feedback as to what the level means, if you have traded any epic or legendary equipment with a fisherman before or even give feedback on what changed since last time you went there.

Power Fantasy is an action roguelike from Lava Lamb Games that embraces one of gaming’s most satisfying concepts: starting weak and slowly transforming into an unstoppable force of destruction. Built around survival-focused gameplay, character progression, and extensive build experimentation, the game enters a genre that has become increasingly crowded in recent years. However, instead of relying purely on familiar mechanics, it separates itself by emphasizing player freedom and meaningful customization systems that make every run feel personal. The overall structure follows a formula that many fans of modern action roguelikes will immediately recognize. Players enter enemy-filled arenas where survival becomes the primary objective. Defeating enemies rewards progression opportunities that steadily increase combat effectiveness. Small decisions early in a run eventually evolve into dramatically different playstyles depending on how upgrades, abilities, and perks combine. The satisfaction comes not only from surviving longer but from watching carefully assembled builds evolve into devastating engines of destruction capable of clearing overwhelming enemy hordes. Character selection immediately introduces variety into the experience. Multiple heroes offer distinct strengths and gameplay styles that influence how players approach combat and progression. Some characters naturally encourage aggressive offensive strategies, while others support more calculated approaches focused on mobility, positioning, or ability combinations. This variation gives each run a stronger sense of identity while encouraging experimentation beyond simply repeating familiar strategies. Progression systems represent one of the game’s strongest qualities. Power Fantasy gives players substantial control over shaping builds through perk selection systems and upgrade mechanics that create meaningful strategic decisions. Instead of relying entirely on random chance, players receive tools that allow stronger influence over progression direction. Reroll systems, perk management options, and build flexibility help reduce frustration while increasing opportunities for experimentation. This balance between randomness and player control creates a satisfying rhythm where successful builds feel earned rather than accidental. Combat embraces spectacle without sacrificing clarity. Early moments often feel tense and vulnerable as players navigate enemy attacks with limited resources and weaker abilities. Over time, however, successful runs gradually shift toward large-scale chaos where enemies flood the screen and carefully assembled builds unleash increasingly destructive combinations. That transformation remains one of the game’s most rewarding aspects because progression feels visible, powerful, and consistently satisfying. Enemy scaling helps maintain engagement throughout longer sessions. Threats increase steadily alongside player power, creating situations where growth feels necessary rather than excessive. The challenge progression prevents combat from becoming completely effortless while preserving the excitement of becoming dramatically stronger over time. Every successful survival attempt reinforces the fantasy promised directly by the game’s title. Replay value receives strong support through unlock systems and progression incentives that reward continued play. Experimenting with different heroes, discovering stronger build combinations, and pushing toward increasingly effective strategies creates long-term motivation. Failed attempts rarely feel meaningless because progression continues beyond individual runs. Incremental advancement strengthens the addictive loop that successful roguelikes depend upon. Visually, Power Fantasy adopts a pixel-art presentation style that prioritizes readability and responsiveness. Combat remains understandable even during more chaotic moments when projectiles, abilities, and enemy groups begin filling large portions of the screen. The visual approach may appear simple initially, but it supports gameplay exceptionally well by ensuring players can react effectively under pressure. Audio presentation complements the action without dominating attention. Sound effects communicate combat impact effectively, while music reinforces pacing during longer sessions. The game wisely prioritizes gameplay flow over cinematic presentation, keeping focus firmly on progression systems and combat execution. One area where players may notice familiarity is overall genre structure. Fans deeply invested in survival roguelikes will likely recognize design ideas shared across similar titles. While Power Fantasy introduces customization strengths and build flexibility that help distinguish it, the foundation remains rooted in established conventions. Players seeking dramatic genre reinvention may find certain systems familiar. Environmental variety could also feel somewhat limited for players investing extensive time into progression. The gameplay systems themselves remain engaging enough to sustain interest, but broader environmental diversity might further strengthen long-term replayability. Despite those limitations, Power Fantasy succeeds because it understands what makes progression-focused roguelikes enjoyable. It delivers satisfying growth systems, meaningful player choice, varied hero design, and combat escalation that consistently rewards experimentation. The freedom to shape builds according to personal preference creates stronger investment while helping individual runs feel unique. The game ultimately captures the excitement of watching fragile beginnings evolve into overwhelming power. Every improvement feels meaningful, every successful combination feels rewarding, and every run offers opportunities to discover stronger strategies. For players who enjoy action roguelikes built around experimentation, progression, and the thrill of becoming absurdly powerful over time, Power Fantasy delivers a polished and highly enjoyable experience. Rating: 8/10
